claim: DTD's active site architecture is unable to discriminate between D-amino acids and achiral glycine due to strict L-chiral rejection through Gly-cisPro motif during chiral proofreading.
source: Strict L-chiral rejection through Gly-cisPro motif during chiral proofreading underlies the inability of D-aminoacyl-tRNA deacylase (DTD) to discriminate between D-amino acids and achiral glycine.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to previous work on DTD's mechanism.

claim: The Gly-tRNAGly 'misediting paradox' is resolved by EF-Tu in the cell.
source: The consequent Gly-tRNAGly 'misediting paradox' is resolved by EF-Tu in the cell.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references prior work (Routh et al., 2016).

claim: DTD can edit mischarged Gly-tRNAAla species four orders of magnitude more efficiently than AlaRS.
source: Here, we show that DTD's active site architecture can efficiently edit mischarged Gly-tRNAAla species four orders of magnitude more efficiently than even AlaRS, the only ubiquitous cellular checkpoint known for clearing the error.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: DTD knockout in AlaRS editing-defective background causes pronounced toxicity in Escherichia coli even at low-glycine levels.
source: Also, DTD knockout in AlaRS editing-defective background causes pronounced toxicity in Escherichia coli even at low-glycine levels which is alleviated by alanine supplementation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Alanine supplementation alleviates the toxicity caused by DTD knockout in AlaRS editing-defective background at low-glycine levels.
source: Also, DTD knockout in AlaRS editing-defective background causes pronounced toxicity in Escherichia coli even at low-glycine levels which is alleviated by alanine supplementation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: DTD positively selects the universally invariant tRNAAla-specific G3•U70 wobble base pair.
source: We further demonstrate that DTD positively selects the universally invariant tRNAAla-specific G3•U70.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: DTD's activity on non-cognate Gly-tRNAAla is conserved across all bacteria and eukaryotes.
source: Moreover, DTD's activity on non-cognate Gly-tRNAAla is conserved across all bacteria and eukaryotes, suggesting DTD's key cellular role as a glycine deacylator.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: DTD has a key cellular role as a glycine deacylator.
source: Moreover, DTD's activity on non-cognate Gly-tRNAAla is conserved across all bacteria and eukaryotes, suggesting DTD's key cellular role as a glycine deacylator.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of DTD's activity on Gly-tRNAAla across bacteria and eukaryotes.

claim: DTD is a key factor that keeps chiral errors away from the translational machinery by allowing only L-amino acids to form proteins.
source: D-aminoacyl-tRNA deacylase (DTD) is a key factor that keeps chiral errors away from the translational machinery by allowing only L-amino acids to form proteins and has therefore been implicated in perpetuation of homochirality in the protein world (Calendar and Berg, 1967; Soutourina et al., 1999, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: DTD has been implicated in perpetuation of homochirality in the protein world.
source: D-aminoacyl-tRNA deacylase (DTD) is a key factor that keeps chiral errors away from the translational machinery by allowing only L-amino acids to form proteins and has therefore been implicated in perpetuation of homochirality in the protein world (Calendar and Berg, 1967; Soutourina et al., 1999, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: DTD's enantioselection involves only strict L-chiral rejection, rather than D-chiral selection.
source: The design principle by which this remarkable configurational specificity is achieved by DTD involves only strict L-chiral rejection, rather than D-chiral selection.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work (Ahmad et al., 2013).

claim: An invariant cross-subunit Gly-cisPro motif forms the structural and mechanistic basis for DTD's enantioselection.
source: An invariant cross-subunit Gly-cisPro motif forms the structural and mechanistic basis for DTD's enantioselection (Ahmad et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The architecture of DTD's chiral proofreading site cannot prevent misediting of achiral glycine charged on tRNAGly.
source: Thus, the architecture of DTD's chiral proofreading site is such that it cannot prevent misediting of achiral glycine charged on tRNAGly and seems to have an inherent flaw.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work (Routh et al., 2016).

claim: The glycine 'misediting paradox' is effectively resolved through protection of the cognate achiral substrate by elongation factor thermo unstable (EF-Tu).
source: The glycine 'misediting paradox' is, however, effectively resolved through protection of the cognate achiral substrate by elongation factor thermo unstable (EF-Tu) (Routh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: About half of the 20 aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases have editing functions to rectify incorrect pairing of a similar non-cognate L-amino acid with a tRNA.
source: While occasional chiral errors that occur during aminoacylation are cleared by DTD to ensure the accuracy of aminoacyl-tRNAs present in the cellular pool, a major role is played by editing functions associated with about half of the 20 aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (aaRSs) to rectify the incorrect pairing of a similar non-cognate L-amino acid with a tRNA (Guo and Schimmel, 2012; Ibba and Soll, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: AaRSs can edit the non-cognate amino acid at the aminoacylation site itself after the amino acid has been activated but prior to its transfer to the tRNA (pre-transfer editing).
source: These aaRSs can edit the non-cognate amino acid at the aminoacylation site itself after the amino acid has been activated (i.e. formation of aminoacyl-AMP using ATP as a substrate) but prior to its transfer to the tRNA (pre-transfer editing).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge about aaRS editing mechanisms.

claim: Proofreading can happen at a distinct editing site after the activated non-cognate amino acid has been esterified with the tRNA (post-transfer editing).
source: Alternatively, proofreading can happen at a distinct editing site after the activated non-cognate amino acid has been esterified with the tRNA (post-transfer editing).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge about aaRS editing mechanisms.

claim: Even mild defects in proofreading can lead to adverse cellular outcomes like cell growth retardation, neurodegeneration, cardiomyopathy and cell death.
source: These proofreading processes are so crucial that even mild defects can lead to adverse cellular outcomes like cell growth retardation, neurodegeneration, cardiomyopathy and cell death (Bacher et al., 2005; Bullwinkle et al., 2014; Karkhanis et al., 2007; Korencic et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2014; Moghal et al., 2016; Nangle et al., 2002; Roy et al., 2004), although a compromise in editing can also be beneficial as it helps the organism to tide over stress conditions (Moghal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: A compromise in editing can be beneficial as it helps the organism to tide over stress conditions.
source: These proofreading processes are so crucial that even mild defects can lead to adverse cellular outcomes like cell growth retardation, neurodegeneration, cardiomyopathy and cell death (Bacher et al., 2005; Bullwinkle et al., 2014; Karkhanis et al., 2007; Korencic et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2014; Moghal et al., 2016; Nangle et al., 2002; Roy et al., 2004), although a compromise in editing can also be beneficial as it helps the organism to tide over stress conditions (Moghal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Glycine is misactivated by alanyl-tRNA synthetase (AlaRS) at a frequency of 1/240 relative to alanine.
source: Being comparatively small and similar to the cognate alanine, glycine and serine are misactivated by alanyl-tRNA synthetase (AlaRS) at significantly high frequencies of 1/240 and 1/500, respectively, relative to alanine (Tsui and Fersht, 1981) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work, and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Serine is misactivated by alanyl-tRNA synthetase (AlaRS) at a frequency of 1/500 relative to alanine.
source: Being comparatively small and similar to the cognate alanine, glycine and serine are misactivated by alanyl-tRNA synthetase (AlaRS) at significantly high frequencies of 1/240 and 1/500, respectively, relative to alanine (Tsui and Fersht, 1981) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work, and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The misactivation rates of glycine and serine by AlaRS are much higher than the overall error rates of ~10−4–10−3 observed during protein biosynthesis.
source: However, these misactivation rates are much higher than the overall error rates of ~10−4–10−3 observed during protein biosynthesis (Ogle and Ramakrishnan, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Once misactivated, non-cognate amino acids are mischarged on tRNAAla by AlaRS.
source: Once (mis)activated, these non-cognate amino acids are mischarged on tRNAAla by AlaRS.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents a logical consequence of misactivation.

claim: The editing domain of AlaRS has to specifically remove two non-cognate amino acids—the larger serine and the smaller glycine—attached to tRNAAla without acting on the cognate alanine, which is intermediate in size between serine and glycine.
source: This creates a unique mechanistic challenge for the editing domain of AlaRS, which has to specifically remove two non-cognate amino acids—the larger serine and the smaller glycine—attached to tRNAAla without acting on the cognate alanine, which is intermediate in size between serine and glycine.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents a logical analysis of the editing challenge.

claim: The double-discrimination problem of AlaRS is 3.5-billion-year-old and unavoidable for AlaRS in all forms of life.
source: This 3.5-billion-year-old double-discrimination problem is shown to be unavoidable for AlaRS in all forms of life (Guo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Serine mischarging on tRNAAla is detrimental to the cell.
source: It has also been shown that serine mischarging on tRNAAla is detrimental to the cell and even a mild deficiency in the proofreading activity of AlaRS leads to cell death and severe neuropathologies in mouse (Lee et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Even a mild deficiency in the proofreading activity of AlaRS leads to cell death and severe neuropathologies in mouse.
source: It has also been shown that serine mischarging on tRNAAla is detrimental to the cell and even a mild deficiency in the proofreading activity of AlaRS leads to cell death and severe neuropathologies in mouse (Lee et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Several standalone trans-editing modules (collectively called AlaXs), which are homologous to AlaRS cis-editing domain, have come into being.
source: The problem is so severe that several standalone trans-editing modules (collectively called AlaXs), which are homologous to AlaRS cis-editing domain, have come into being.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge about AlaX proteins.

claim: Trans-editing factors AlaXs are not ubiquitously present; their distribution is more in archaea than in eukaryotes and bacteria.
source: However, these trans-editing factors are not ubiquitously present; their distribution is more in archaea than in eukaryotes and bacteria (Guo and Schimmel, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Only archaeal AlaXs are known to clear both Ser-tRNAAla and Gly-tRNAAla.
source: Surprisingly, only archaeal AlaXs are known to clear both Ser-tRNAAla and Gly-tRNAAla (Ahel et al., 2003); eukaryotic AlaXs have been shown to act as cellular redundancies to edit only Ser-tRNAAla (Guo et al., 2009), whereas biochemical activity of bacterial AlaXs is yet to be probed (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work, and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Eukaryotic AlaXs have been shown to act as cellular redundancies to edit only Ser-tRNAAla.
source: Surprisingly, only archaeal AlaXs are known to clear both Ser-tRNAAla and Gly-tRNAAla (Ahel et al., 2003); eukaryotic AlaXs have been shown to act as cellular redundancies to edit only Ser-tRNAAla (Guo et al., 2009), whereas biochemical activity of bacterial AlaXs is yet to be probed (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work, and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Biochemical activity of bacterial AlaXs is yet to be probed.
source: Surprisingly, only archaeal AlaXs are known to clear both Ser-tRNAAla and Gly-tRNAAla (Ahel et al., 2003); eukaryotic AlaXs have been shown to act as cellular redundancies to edit only Ser-tRNAAla (Guo et al., 2009), whereas biochemical activity of bacterial AlaXs is yet to be probed (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents a gap in knowledge.

claim: Only serine mischarging by AlaRS was believed to pose the major threat to the cell.
source: These findings corroborated the notion that only serine mischarging by AlaRS poses the major threat to the cell (Guo et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: There is significant glycine mischarging by AlaRS in the presence of EF-Tu.
source: In the current study, we show that there is significant glycine mischarging by AlaRS in the presence of EF-Tu which can be equally pernicious as serine mischarging.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Glycine mischarging by AlaRS can be equally pernicious as serine mischarging.
source: In the current study, we show that there is significant glycine mischarging by AlaRS in the presence of EF-Tu which can be equally pernicious as serine mischarging.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: In comparison to alanine charging, significant glycine mischarging was observed in aminoacylation assays in the presence of EF-Tu.
source: To test whether Gly-tRNAAla is accumulated due to mischarging of glycine on tRNAAla by AlaRS, we performed aminoacylation assays in the presence of EF-Tu. In comparison to alanine charging, significant glycine mischarging was observed.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The level of glycine mischarging was about twice that of serine mischarging in aminoacylation assays in the presence of EF-Tu.
source: Furthermore, the level of glycine mischarging was about twice that of serine mischarging (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Even with full AlaRS editing potential, there can be significant accumulation of Gly-tRNAAla species in the cell.
source: This clearly indicated that even with full AlaRS editing potential, there can be significant accumulation of Gly-tRNAAla species in the cell.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The twofold higher level of glycine mischarging compared to serine is in accordance with the twofold higher misactivation rate of glycine by AlaRS when compared to that of serine.
source: Moreover, this is in accordance with the twofold higher misactivation rate of glycine by AlaRS when compared to that of serine (Tsui and Fersht, 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: When AlaRS editing was compromised, the accumulation of Gly-tRNAAla was significantly high, almost equal to the level of Ala-tRNAAla formation.
source: We then checked the accumulation of Gly-tRNAAla when AlaRS editing was compromised, and it was found to be significantly high, almost equal to the level of Ala-tRNAAla formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A known editing site mutation (C666A) in AlaRS from Escherichia coli was used to accomplish a compromise in the proofreading activity of AlaRS.
source: To accomplish a compromise in the proofreading activity of AlaRS, a known editing site mutation (viz., C666A) in AlaRS from Escherichia coli was used (Beebe et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Based on structural considerations and evolutionary substitution patterns of alanine, substitution of glycine for alanine is more detrimental than substitution of serine.
source: Furthermore, based on structural considerations and evolutionary substitution patterns of alanine, where it is replaced more by serine than by glycine (Betts et al., 2003), it is to be expected that substitution of glycine for alanine is more detrimental than substitution of serine.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The activity of DTD on Gly-tRNAAla was ~1000-fold more than that on Gly-tRNAGly.
source: The leads for the solution to this puzzle came when, surprisingly, we found that the activity of DTD on Gly-tRNAAla was ~1000-fold more than that on Gly-tRNAGly (as discussed later).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: DTD could easily edit Gly-tRNAAla in the presence of EF-Tu even though the ratio of activated EF-Tu to DTD in the assays was much higher than the cellular ratio.
source: Moreover, although the ratio of activated EF-Tu to DTD in our assays (viz., ~200 nM to 5 or 10 pM) was much higher than the cellular ratio (viz., ~200:1) (Li et al., 2014), DTD could easily edit Gly-tRNAAla in the presence of EF-Tu (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: EF-Tu showed significant protection of the cognate Gly-tRNAGly from DTD.
source: This was unlike the case of Gly-tRNAGly, wherein EF-Tu showed significant protection of the cognate achiral substrate from DTD (Routh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ~20,000 times more AlaRS as compared to DTD was required for similar kind of deacylation of Gly-tRNAAla under identical conditions.
source: The deacylation of Gly-tRNAAla by DTD was so striking that ~20,000 times more AlaRS (which is the only universally occurring editing factor for Gly-tRNAAla) as compared to DTD was required for similar kind of deacylation under identical conditions (Figures 2b and 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2b and 3b.

claim: AlaRS is the only universally occurring editing factor for Gly-tRNAAla.
source: The deacylation of Gly-tRNAAla by DTD was so striking that ~20,000 times more AlaRS (which is the only universally occurring editing factor for Gly-tRNAAla) as compared to DTD was required for similar kind of deacylation under identical conditions (Figures 2b and 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and represents established knowledge.

claim: AlaRS showed a significant decrease in deacylation activity on Gly-tRNAAla when tested in the presence of EF-Tu.
source: In addition, unlike DTD, AlaRS showed a significant decrease in deacylation activity on Gly-tRNAAla when tested in the presence of EF-Tu (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a,b.

claim: DTD is efficient in eliminating Gly-tRNAAla despite the presence of EF-Tu.
source: Moreover, our assays demonstrated that DTD is not only efficient in eliminating Gly-tRNAAla despite the presence of EF-Tu (Figure 2b) but can also very effectively prevent the accumulation of Gly-tRNAAla during aminoacylation by AlaRS in the presence of EF-Tu (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: DTD can very effectively prevent the accumulation of Gly-tRNAAla during aminoacylation by AlaRS in the presence of EF-Tu.
source: Moreover, our assays demonstrated that DTD is not only efficient in eliminating Gly-tRNAAla despite the presence of EF-Tu (Figure 2b) but can also very effectively prevent the accumulation of Gly-tRNAAla during aminoacylation by AlaRS in the presence of EF-Tu (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: DTD deacylated Gly-tRNAAla even in the presence of EF-Tu and AlaRS at just 10 pM concentration of DTD in both aminoacylation and deacylation conditions.
source: To this end, we performed competition assays involving AlaRS, DTD and EF-Tu. In both aminoacylation and deacylation conditions, we found that DTD deacylated Gly-tRNAAla even in the presence of EF-Tu and AlaRS at just 10 pM concentration of DTD (Figures 2a and 3c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2a and 3c.

claim: The cellular ratio of DTD to AlaRS is ~1:5.
source: Considering the cellular ratio of DTD to AlaRS (viz, ~1:5) (Li et al., 2014) and their relative activities on Gly-tRNAAla, it is evident that when DTD is present, it will eliminate Gly-tRNAAla more efficiently than AlaRS if the non-cognate achiral substrate is released in solution from the synthetase.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: When DTD is present, it will eliminate Gly-tRNAAla more efficiently than AlaRS if the non-cognate achiral substrate is released in solution from the synthetase.
source: Considering the cellular ratio of DTD to AlaRS (viz, ~1:5) (Li et al., 2014) and their relative activities on Gly-tRNAAla, it is evident that when DTD is present, it will eliminate Gly-tRNAAla more efficiently than AlaRS if the non-cognate achiral substrate is released in solution from the synthetase.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from experimental data and cellular ratios.

claim: Compared to Class I synthetases, enzymes belonging to Class II have been shown to have faster product release rates.
source: In this context, it is important to note that compared to Class I synthetases, enzymes belonging to Class II, which include AlaRS, have been shown to have faster product release rates (Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Class II aaRSs require resampling of the released mischarged product to edit the cytosolic pool of mischarged tRNAs.
source: Hence, Class II aaRSs require resampling of the released mischarged product to edit the cytosolic pool of mischarged tRNAs (Ling et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: It would be very difficult for the CCA-arm at the 3′ end of tRNAAla harboring the non-cognate amino acid to flip from the aminoacylation site to the editing site without undergoing major conformational changes.
source: This makes even more sense as regards AlaRS, since our structural analysis of AlaRS in complex with tRNAAla (PDB id: 3WQY) suggests that it would be very difficult for the CCA-arm at the 3′ end of tRNAAla harboring the non-cognate amino acid to flip from the aminoacylation site to the editing site without undergoing major conformational changes (Naganuma et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and based on structural analysis and citation to previous work.

claim: A significant fraction of Gly-tRNAAla and Ser-tRNAAla is released from AlaRS prior to their recapture for proofreading by the cis-editing domain.
source: Such a dynamics would naturally facilitate a faster release of the misacylated product in solution, implying that a significant fraction of Gly-tRNAAla and Ser-tRNAAla is released from AlaRS prior to their recapture for proofreading by the cis-editing domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from structural and kinetic considerations.

claim: The problem of glycine mischarging by AlaRS would have been so detrimental that a highly efficient factor like DTD was required to be employed for this function in addition to AlaRS editing domain.
source: Overall, the above data suggest that the problem of glycine mischarging by AlaRS would have been so detrimental that a highly efficient factor like DTD was required to be employed for this function in addition to AlaRS editing domain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Earlier in vivo studies had shown that AlaRS editing defect causes glycine toxicity only at very high levels of glycine supplementation (80 mM) as opposed to serine which causes toxicity at significantly lower levels (2.5 mM).
source: Earlier in vivo studies had shown that AlaRS editing defect causes glycine toxicity only at very high levels of glycine supplementation (80 mM) as opposed to serine which causes toxicity at significantly lower levels (2.5 mM) (Beebe et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Previous studies showing glycine toxicity only at high levels were carried out in strains harboring DTD, explaining the need for supplementation with more glycine to show toxicity.
source: It is worth noting that these studies were carried out in strains harboring DTD, hence explaining the need for supplementation with more glycine to show toxicity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from the experimental design of previous studies.

claim: An E. coli strain was generated in which dtd (the gene encoding DTD) was knocked out in the background of editing-defective AlaRS.
source: To check if the absence of DTD makes E. coli susceptible to glycine, we generated an E. coli strain in which dtd (the gene encoding DTD) was knocked out in the background of editing-defective AlaRS.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and describes the experimental approach.

claim: To create a strain that was completely devoid of AlaRS editing activity, the genomic copy of AlaRS gene (alaS) was knocked out and a triple-mutant AlaRS (viz., T567F/S587W/C666F) was expressed from a plasmid.
source: To create a strain that was completely devoid of AlaRS editing activity, the genomic copy of AlaRS gene (alaS) was knocked out and a triple-mutant AlaRS (viz., T567F/S587W/C666F) was expressed from a plasmid.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and describes the experimental approach.

claim: The editing site mutations in AlaRS were designed on the basis of a structural (homology) model of E. coli AlaRS cis-editing domain that was generated using the structure of Archaeoglobus fulgidus AlaRS (PDB id: 2ZTG) as a template.
source: The editing site mutations were designed on the basis of a structural (homology) model of E. coli AlaRS cis-editing domain that was generated using the structure of Archaeoglobus fulgidus AlaRS (PDB id: 2ZTG) as a template.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and describes the experimental approach.

claim: Three residues in the proposed editing site were supplanted by bulkier residues to occlude the pocket and prevent substrate binding.
source: Three residues in the proposed editing site (Beebe et al., 2003; Sokabe et al., 2005) were supplanted by bulkier residues to occlude the pocket and prevent substrate binding (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 4a,b.

claim: The triple-mutant AlaRS was found to be inactive on both Ser-tRNAAla and Gly-tRNAAla even when the protein concentration was increased to 1500-fold that of wild-type AlaRS.
source: The triple-mutant was found to be inactive on both Ser-tRNAAla and Gly-tRNAAla even when the protein concentration was increased to 1500-fold that of wild-type AlaRS (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c,d.

claim: Previously known editing-defective mutants of AlaRS (C666A and C666A/Q584H) showed significant activity at just 10-fold higher concentration of the enzyme.
source: It is worth mentioning here that the previously known editing-defective mutants of AlaRS (C666A and C666A/Q584H) (Beebe et al., 2003), when checked for deacylation activity on both Ser-tRNAAla and Gly-tRNAAla, were found to show significant activity at just 10-fold higher concentration of the enzyme (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c,d.

claim: The DTD knockout strain in the background of AlaRS editing defect showed some toxicity even without any amino acid supplementation.
source: Cellular toxicity studies using spot dilution assays and growth curve analysis with the DTD knockout strain in the background of AlaRS editing defect showed some toxicity even without any amino acid supplementation, and the toxicity increased with glycine supplementation as low as 3 mM.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The toxicity in the DTD knockout strain in the background of AlaRS editing defect increased with glycine supplementation as low as 3 mM.
source: Cellular toxicity studies using spot dilution assays and growth curve analysis with the DTD knockout strain in the background of AlaRS editing defect showed some toxicity even without any amino acid supplementation, and the toxicity increased with glycine supplementation as low as 3 mM.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: At 10 mM of glycine supplementation, the cells showed severe growth defect.
source: At 10 mM of glycine supplementation, the cells showed severe growth defect (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Alanine supplementation completely recovered the toxicity caused by glycine and rescued the growth completely.
source: To check whether this was specifically due to mischarging caused by AlaRS, toxicity experiments were carried out in the presence of alanine, since the latter is expected to compete for the AlaRS aminoacylation site during charging of tRNAAla. It was observed that alanine supplementation completely recovered the toxicity caused by glycine and rescued the growth completely (Figure 5b,c,d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b,c,d.

claim: Histidine failed to rescue the cells from glycine toxicity.
source: Moreover, to rule out any non-specific effects due to amino acid supplementation, histidine was used as a negative control, and it was found that it failed to rescue the cells from glycine toxicity (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c,d.

claim: DTD was found to be totally inactive on Ser-tRNAAla in biochemical assays.
source: Furthermore, DTD was found to be totally inactive on Ser-tRNAAla in our biochemical assays which confirmed that the toxicity observed in the DTD-lacking cells in the background of AlaRS editing defect was not due to serine mischarging on tRNAAla by AlaRS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The toxicity observed in the DTD-lacking cells in the background of AlaRS editing defect was not due to serine mischarging on tRNAAla by AlaRS.
source: Furthermore, DTD was found to be totally inactive on Ser-tRNAAla in our biochemical assays which confirmed that the toxicity observed in the DTD-lacking cells in the background of AlaRS editing defect was not due to serine mischarging on tRNAAla by AlaRS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: DTD's chiral proofreading site rejects even L-alanine, the smallest L-chiral substrate.
source: The above observation is expected since it has been shown earlier that DTD's chiral proofreading site rejects even L-alanine, the smallest L-chiral substrate (Routh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: DTD acts as a key cellular factor that edits glycine mischarged on tRNAAla by AlaRS.
source: Taken together, these experiments established that DTD acts as a key cellular factor that edits glycine mischarged on tRNAAla by AlaRS.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: No toxicity of glycine supplementation was observed in E. coli MG1655 ∆dtd strain in the background of wild-type AlaRS.
source: However, no toxicity of glycine supplementation was observed in E. coli MG1655 ∆dtd strain in the background of wild-type AlaRS (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Under normal growth conditions, AlaRS editing is sufficient for the cell to survive.
source: This indicates that under normal growth conditions, AlaRS editing is sufficient for the cell to survive.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The errors produced because of the absence of DTD are possibly tolerated by E. coli under laboratory conditions.
source: The errors produced because of the absence of DTD are possibly tolerated by E. coli under laboratory conditions, as has been noted in several other cases of editing function of aaRSs (Reynolds et al., 2010a, 2010b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Defects in error correction are known to manifest in toxic effects only in special growth conditions like oxidative stress, oxygen deprivation, starvation/nutrient limiting conditions etc.
source: The real implications of editing defects are only recently being appreciated in some specific growth conditions like oxidative stress, oxygen deprivation, starvation/nutrient limiting conditions etc. (Bullwinkle et al., 2014; Cvetesic et al., 2014; Kermgard et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: DTD had more than 10-fold increased activity on Gly-tRNAGly harboring G3•U70 as compared to the wild-type achiral cognate substrate.
source: To test this hypothesis, we transplanted G3•U70 at the same position in tRNAGly. We found that DTD had more than 10-fold increased activity on Gly-tRNAGly harboring G3•U70 as compared to the wild-type achiral cognate substrate (Figure 6a,c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a,c.

claim: Substitution of the G3•C70 in the wild-type Gly-tRNAGly with A3•U70 did not cause any increase in the activity of DTD.
source: To strengthen this hypothesis, we substituted the G3•C70 in the wild-type Gly-tRNAGly with the other Watson-Crick base pair, that is A3•U70. This substitution did not cause any increase in the activity of DTD (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The G3•U70 wobble base pair, which is a universally conserved feature of tRNAAla, acts as a positive determinant for DTD.
source: This clearly suggests that the G3•U70 wobble base pair, which is a universally conserved feature of tRNAAla, acts as a positive determinant for DTD.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: There are other features in tRNAAla distinct from tRNAGly that account for the higher activity of DTD on tRNAAla when compared to tRNAGly.
source: It also suggests the existence of other features in tRNAAla distinct from tRNAGly that accounts for the higher activity of DTD on tRNAAla when compared to tRNAGly, and this aspect requires further exploration.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from experimental data.

claim: G3•U70 is unique to and one of the major identity elements of tRNAAla across all life forms.
source: Since G3•U70 is unique to and one of the major identity elements of tRNAAla across all life forms (Hou and Schimmel, 1988; 1989; McClain and Foss, 1988; Ripmaster et al., 1995; Shiba et al., 1995), we envisaged that DTD could be positively selecting tRNAAla using the wobble base pair.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The specificity of AlaRS for G3•U70 is so robust that incorporation of this base pair into other tRNAs or minihelices converts non-alanine-accepting tRNAs to be recognized and charged by AlaRS.
source: The specificity of AlaRS for G3•U70 is so robust that incorporation of this base pair into other tRNAs or minihelices converts non-alanine-accepting tRNAs to be recognized and charged by AlaRS (Musier-Forsyth and Schimmel, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The G3•U70-based selection of tRNAAla by DTD indicates towards the role of DTD in editing Gly-tRNAAla even before the recruitment of AlaRS editing domains.
source: The G3•U70-based selection of tRNAAla by DTD clearly indicates towards the role of DTD in editing Gly-tRNAAla even before the recruitment of AlaRS editing domains, which have primarily evolved to remove serine mischarged on tRNAAla (Novoa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from experimental data and evolutionary considerations.

claim: AlaRS editing domains have primarily evolved to remove serine mischarged on tRNAAla.
source: The G3•U70-based selection of tRNAAla by DTD clearly indicates towards the role of DTD in editing Gly-tRNAAla even before the recruitment of AlaRS editing domains, which have primarily evolved to remove serine mischarged on tRNAAla (Novoa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Modulation of DTD's activity depending on tRNA elements is counter-intuitive as DTD is expected to act on multiple tRNAs with comparable efficiencies.
source: Furthermore, modulation of DTD's activity depending on tRNA elements is counter-intuitive as DTD is expected to act on multiple tRNAs with comparable efficiencies.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and represents a logical consideration.

claim: The present work has unveiled a completely new aspect of DTD's aminoacyl-tRNA recognition code in which the role of the amino acid as well as the tRNA component needs to be looked at separately.
source: Hence, the present work has unveiled a completely new aspect of DTD's aminoacyl-tRNA recognition code in which the role of the amino acid as well as the tRNA component needs to be looked at separately.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from experimental data.

claim: A recognition code exists for EF-Tu, wherein three successive base pairs in the T-stem of tRNA thermodynamically compensate for the differential binding affinity of EF-Tu toward different amino acids.
source: Interestingly, a recognition code exists for EF-Tu, wherein three successive base pairs in the T-stem of tRNA thermodynamically compensate for the differential binding affinity of EF-Tu toward different amino acids (LaRiviere et al., 2001; Roy et al., 2007; Sanderson and Uhlenbeck, 2007b; Schrader et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Significant differences were found in residues around the chiral proofreading site of DTD which are believed to interact with the acceptor stem of tRNA.
source: DTD's ubiquitous presence in bacteria and eukaryotes prompted us to test whether its role in clearing mischarged Gly-tRNAAla, in addition to its role in proofreading D-aminoacyl-tRNAs, is conserved in these two domains of life. It is important to investigate this aspect because we found significant differences in residues—which are believed to interact with the acceptor stem of tRNA—around the chiral proofreading site of DTD.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only 7 out of 20 residues in the selected region around DTD's active site are invariant across bacterial and eukaryotic DTDs.
source: Notably, only 7 out of 20 residues in the selected region are invariant across bacterial and eukaryotic DTDs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: DTDs from different eukaryotes (Leishmania major, Drosophila melanogaster, Danio rerio, Plasmodium falciparum) and E. coli were found to act effectively on both bacterial and eukaryotic tRNAs at 10 pM of DTD concentration.
source: To ascertain this, we tested DTDs from different eukaryotes—Leishmania major (LmDTD), Drosophila melanogaster (DmDTD) and Danio rerio (DrDTD)—spanning the entire spectrum of unicellular, invertebrate and vertebrate species, in addition to DTDs from Plasmodium falciparum (PfDTD) and E. coli (EcDTD). These DTDs were tested on glycine mischarged on both E. coli tRNAAla and D. melanogaster tRNAAla (Figure 7). All these DTDs were found to act effectively on both bacterial and eukaryotic tRNAs at 10 pM of DTD concentration.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: In spite of the cross-species differences in DTD and tRNAAla, DTD's activity on Gly-tRNAAla is most likely conserved throughout bacteria and eukaryotes.
source: This indicates that in spite of the cross-species differences in DTD and tRNAAla, DTD's activity on Gly-tRNAAla is most likely conserved throughout bacteria and eukaryotes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: This study provides an unprecedented solution to a fundamental and long-standing puzzle by elucidating a hitherto unknown and physiologically important function of DTD.
source: This study provides an unprecedented solution to a fundamental and long-standing puzzle by elucidating a hitherto unknown and physiologically important function of DTD, which was till now implicated only in enforcing homochirality during translation of the genetic code.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and summarizes the main finding.

claim: The discovery of DTD as a key cellular factor for the elimination of Gly-tRNAAla provides an elegant explanation as to why glycine mischarging by AlaRS was not encountered or considered as a cellular hazard in all the previous studies.
source: The discovery of DTD as a key cellular factor for the elimination of Gly-tRNAAla provides an elegant explanation as to why glycine mischarging by AlaRS was not encountered or considered as a cellular hazard in all the previous studies.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Nature was forced to devise and retain throughout evolution a key checkpoint in the form of DTD that is more efficient than even AlaRS's proofreading function to tackle the glycine mischarging problem.
source: Our study thus brings forth the criticality of glycine mischarging problem, which was largely overlooked and underappreciated prior to this work. It also reveals that nature was forced to devise and retain throughout evolution a key checkpoint in the form of DTD that is more efficient than even AlaRS's proofreading function to tackle this problem (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The necessity of keeping DTD's active site design intact during the course of evolution was probably because removal of the mischarged Gly-tRNAAla species from the cellular pool took precedence over DTD's unwarranted activity on Gly-tRNAGly.
source: The study also highlights the necessity of keeping DTD's active site design intact during the course of evolution, probably because removal of the mischarged Gly-tRNAAla species from the cellular pool took precedence over DTD's unwarranted activity on Gly-tRNAGly.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The glycine 'misediting paradox' was effectively resolved by safeguarding the cognate achiral substrate using EF-Tu as well as keeping the cellular levels of DTD low and tightly regulated.
source: Nevertheless, the glycine 'misediting paradox' was effectively resolved by safeguarding the cognate achiral substrate using EF-Tu as well as keeping the cellular levels of DTD low and tightly regulated (Routh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: What seemed to be an apparent flaw in the architecture of DTD's active site proved to be a necessity.
source: Thus, what seemed to be an apparent flaw in the architecture of DTD's active site proved to be a necessity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The dual activity of DTD on both achiral and D-chiral substrates depicts it as a plausible 'connecting link' or 'bridging factor' between D-chirality–based and the canonical L-chirality–based proofreading during protein biosynthesis.
source: Moreover, the dual activity of DTD on both achiral and D-chiral substrates depicts it as a plausible 'connecting link' or 'bridging factor' between D-chirality–based and the canonical L-chirality–based proofreading during protein biosynthesis (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and represents a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: A DTD-like fold appended to archaeal threonyl-tRNA synthetase (ThrRS) as the N-terminal editing domain (NTD) is specific for editing L-serine mischarged on tRNAThr.
source: This view gains support from the fact that a DTD-like fold appended to archaeal threonyl-tRNA synthetase (ThrRS) as the N-terminal editing domain (NTD) is specific for editing L-serine mischarged on tRNAThr (Ahmad et al., 2015; Dwivedi et al., 2005; Hussain et al., 2006, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The DTD-like fold present in two functional contexts—as NTD in archaea, and as DTD in bacteria and eukaryotes—operates majorly through main chain-mediated contacts for substrate recognition and performs catalysis through RNA, suggesting its primordial origins.
source: It is also worth noting here that the DTD-like fold present in two functional contexts—as NTD in archaea, and as DTD in bacteria and eukaryotes—operates majorly through main chain-mediated contacts for substrate recognition and performs catalysis through RNA, suggesting its primordial origins (Ahmad et al., 2013, 2015; Routh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Glycine mischarging by AlaRS is inevitable and is a classic case of error made by the aminoacylation site of aaRS.
source: Glycine mischarging by AlaRS is inevitable and is a classic case of error made by the aminoacylation site of aaRS, whereas serine mischarging is an offshoot of amino group selection for alanine (Guo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citation to previous work.
